Q000431.stem: A company runs an app on EC2 and a database on Amazon RDS. An auditor asks who is responsible for OS patching in each case and for security group rules. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: AWS patches the EC2 guest OS on request; the customer patches the RDS database engine
Customer: EC2 guest OS and all SGs; AWS: the RDS operating system
AWS patches both guest operating systems
The customer patches both guest operating systems; AWS manages the security groups

Q000431.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With EC2 (IaaS) the customer owns everything from the guest OS up: patches, software, and security group rules. With RDS, a managed service, AWS patches the underlying OS and database engine (in maintenance windows), but network access controls such as security groups remain the customer's responsibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS patching the EC2 guest OS: EC2 is customer-managed from the OS up.
• Customer patching RDS's OS: customers have no OS access on RDS; AWS handles it.
• 'On request' patching: there is no such model. Customers can use Systems Manager Patch Manager themselves.

Key takeaway: responsibility shifts toward AWS as services become more managed, but configuration of access (SGs, IAM, encryption choices) always stays with the customer.

Q000432.stem: An attacker phished the root user's password for a company account, but the login attempt failed. Which control MOST likely stopped it, and what else should be done with the root user?

choices.text: An IAM password policy; also share the root password only with two administrators
MFA on root; also delete root access keys
An SCP denying all root actions in the management account; also enable CloudTrail
A permissions boundary on the root user; also rotate its access keys monthly

Q000432.explanation:
Why this is correct:
MFA requires a second factor beyond the password, so a stolen password alone can't sign in. Best practice is also to delete root access keys and reserve the root user for the few tasks only it can perform.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permissions boundaries: can't be applied to the root user.
• SCPs: don't apply to the management account, and they don't stop sign-in.
• Password policy: applies to IAM users, not root, and sharing the root password increases risk.

Key takeaway: protect root with MFA, no access keys, and minimal use.

Q000436.stem: A company wants its web tier to survive a data center power failure and also a natural disaster affecting an entire metropolitan area. Latency between web servers and the database must stay low. Which design fits?

choices.text: Instances spread across edge locations, with the database in one Availability Zone
Instances across two Regions, replicating synchronously
Instances across multiple AZs in one Region, plus a DR copy in another Region
Instances in one AZ across racks, plus multiple Local Zones for disaster recovery

Q000436.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AZs are isolated from one another (separate power and facilities) but connected with low latency, so a multi-AZ deployment survives a facility failure while keeping database latency low. A Region-wide disaster needs a copy in another Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Racks and Local Zones: a single AZ fails as a unit, and Local Zones are extensions of a parent Region, not a DR design.
• Edge locations: serve CloudFront and Route 53, not EC2 web tiers.
• Synchronous cross-Region replication: adds high latency to every write.

Key takeaway: AZs are for high availability; Regions are for disaster recovery.

Q000438.stem: A role in Account B must read objects in a bucket in Account A. The role's identity policy allows s3:GetObject on the bucket, but access is denied. The objects use SSE-S3. What is missing?

choices.text: An SCP in Account A that explicitly allows access from Account B
A permissions boundary in Account B that also lists s3:GetObject
A bucket policy in Account A granting the role access
A KMS key policy granting Account B decrypt permissions

Q000438.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account access needs permission on both sides: the identity policy in B (already present) and a resource-based policy in A (the bucket policy) that trusts B's principal. Only resource-based policies can grant access to principals in other accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permissions boundary: only limits permissions; it never grants access.
• SCPs: never grant permissions; they only restrict.
• KMS key policy: SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys, so no KMS policy is involved.

Key takeaway: cross-account = identity policy on the caller side + resource policy on the owner side.

Q000442.stem: A mobile app, a CI system in another cloud, and EC2 instances all need AWS access without storing long-term keys. Which service issues the credentials they would use?

choices.text: AWS STS, issuing temporary credentials via AssumeRole and web-identity APIs
AWS KMS, issuing data keys that authorize API calls for a limited time
IAM, generating new access keys for each session and deleting them afterward
AWS Secrets Manager, rotating a shared IAM user key every hour

Q000442.explanation:
Why this is correct:
STS issues temporary credentials: instance profiles use it for EC2, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for OIDC-based workloads like external CI or mobile identity providers, and AssumeRole for cross-account access. They expire automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS data keys: encrypt data; they aren't API credentials.
• Per-session IAM keys: still long-term keys, and churning them is error-prone.
• Rotating a shared user key: still long-term credentials shared across workloads.

Key takeaway: no long-term keys → STS temporary credentials behind roles.

Q000446.stem: A developer role currently has s3:* on all buckets because 'it's easier'. The team needs the role to upload only to one prefix in one bucket. Which change best applies least privilege, and how can the team find what's actually used?

choices.text: Keep s3:* but add a permissions boundary that allows s3:* on all buckets
Keep s3:* and rely on CloudTrail
Scope to PutObject on the prefix; verify with Access Analyzer
Replace s3:* with AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, since reading is safer than writing

Q000446.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources needed: PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket/prefix/*. Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity, showing which actions were actually used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundary allowing s3:*: doesn't narrow anything.
• Read-only access: removes the needed write permission and still grants reads everywhere.
• CloudTrail only: detection after misuse, not prevention.

Key takeaway: scope both actions and resources, and use usage data to trim.

Q000447.stem: A web server in a public subnet accepts HTTPS. The security group allows inbound 443, and the NACL allows inbound 443 and outbound 443. Clients time out. What is wrong?

choices.text: The stateful security group needs an outbound rule for ephemeral response ports
The NACL needs an inbound ephemeral rule, since replies arrive on ephemeral ports
Security groups are evaluated before NACLs, so the NACL rules are ignored
The NACL must allow outbound ephemeral ports for replies

Q000447.explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless: responses to clients go out to the client's ephemeral port, so outbound rules must allow that range. Security groups are stateful and allow return traffic automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG outbound rule for replies: SGs track connections, so return traffic is already allowed.
• Inbound ephemeral: the replies leave the server; inbound ephemeral matters for connections the server initiates.
• Evaluation order: both layers apply; neither is skipped.

Key takeaway: stateless NACLs need rules in both directions, including ephemeral ports.

Q000449.stem: A public API behind CloudFront and an ALB is regularly hit by large DDoS attacks. The company wants 24/7 help from AWS DDoS experts during attacks and credits for scaling charges caused by attacks. What should it enable?

choices.text: AWS Shield Advanced on the CloudFront distribution and ALB
AWS WAF rate-based rules alone on the distribution
Amazon GuardDuty with automated blocking of attacking IPs
AWS Shield Standard, which is included and covers these needs automatically

Q000449.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced detection and mitigation, access to the Shield Response Team, and DDoS cost protection for scaling charges on protected resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Standard: automatic L3/L4 protection for everyone, but no response team or cost protection.
• WAF rate rules alone: help with HTTP floods, but no expert support or cost protection.
• GuardDuty: threat detection for accounts and workloads, not DDoS mitigation.

Key takeaway: expert DDoS support + cost protection → Shield Advanced.

Q000451.stem: A company must find which of its 400 S3 buckets contain passport numbers and credit card data, and get alerts when new sensitive data appears. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Config rules checking bucket encryption
Amazon Macie automated discovery
Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection findings
Amazon Inspector scans of the buckets' contents

Q000451.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3 using managed data identifiers (such as passport and card numbers) and publishes findings for new discoveries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: finds software vulnerabilities, not data content.
• Config encryption rules: encryption status says nothing about whether data is sensitive.
• GuardDuty S3 Protection: detects suspicious access activity, not data content.

Key takeaway: what's IN the S3 data → Macie; who is ACCESSING it suspiciously → GuardDuty.

Q000455.stem: Instances in a private subnet can't reach the internet. The subnet's route table has only the local route. A NAT gateway exists in a public subnet. What fixes this?

choices.text: Add 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the internet gateway in the private subnet's route table
Add a route to the NAT gateway in the public subnet's route table
Add 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the NAT gateway in the private subnet's route table
Attach a security group to the NAT gateway allowing outbound traffic

Q000455.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Route tables decide where traffic from a subnet goes. The private subnet needs a default route to the NAT gateway, which forwards through the internet gateway from its public subnet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route to IGW from the private subnet: makes the subnet public, which needs public IPs and exposes instances.
• SG on the NAT gateway: NAT gateways don't use security groups.
• Route in the public subnet: the public subnet already routes to the IGW; the private subnet is the problem.

Key takeaway: subnets are public or private because of their route tables.

Q000459.stem: A three-tier app places web servers in public subnets and app servers and databases in private subnets. An auditor asks what actually prevents internet users from reaching the database directly. What is the BEST answer?

choices.text: The database has no public DNS name, so it can't be discovered from the internet
The VPC's CIDR range is private, so internet traffic can't be addressed to it
The NAT gateway blocks all inbound connections to private subnets
The DB subnet has no IGW route, and its SG allows only the app tier's SG

Q000459.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Defense in depth: without an internet gateway route and public IP, there's no inbound path from the internet, and the security group limits access to the app tier.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No public DNS name: obscurity isn't a control.
• NAT gateway: enables outbound only; it isn't the reason inbound fails, and it doesn't filter.
• Private CIDR alone: instances with public IPs in routed subnets are reachable despite private VPC ranges.

Key takeaway: isolation comes from routing plus security groups, not from names or address ranges.

Q000463.stem: A bucket uses SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. Uploads of many small objects start failing with ThrottlingException from KMS during peak hours. What reduces KMS calls without weakening encryption?

choices.text: Switch to SSE-C with client-supplied keys
Enable S3 Bucket Keys for SSE-KMS
Request encryption only on download to halve requests
Use a separate KMS key per object to spread the load

Q000463.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSE-KMS uses envelope encryption, generating a data key through KMS for objects. Bucket Keys create a short-lived bucket-level key from KMS and derive object data keys from it, cutting KMS requests (and cost) substantially while keeping KMS-backed encryption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-C: moves key management to the client, a big change that isn't needed.
• Encrypt on download: S3 encrypts at write; this option doesn't exist.
• Key per object: more keys to manage, and it doesn't reduce request volume.

Key takeaway: high-volume SSE-KMS → Bucket Keys.

Q000464.stem: A company needs free public TLS certificates for an ALB and a CloudFront distribution that renew automatically. Which approach fits, and what is required for CloudFront?

choices.text: ACM certificates exported and installed on the ALB targets; CloudFront uses the same Region's certificate
KMS asymmetric keys configured as TLS keys on both the ALB and CloudFront
Certificates stored in Secrets Manager with a rotation Lambda that re-imports them
ACM certificates with DNS validation; the CloudFront certificate must be in us-east-1

Q000464.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM issues free public certificates for integrated services and renews them automatically when DNS validation stays in place. CloudFront uses certificates from us-east-1.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Exporting public ACM certificates: public ACM certificates can't be exported, and CloudFront needs us-east-1.
• KMS keys: KMS doesn't provide TLS certificates to load balancers.
• Secrets Manager rotation: unnecessary work when ACM renews automatically.

Key takeaway: ALB/CloudFront TLS → ACM (CloudFront certs in us-east-1).

Q000468.stem: A company wants encryption, access, and retention controls applied automatically according to how sensitive each dataset is. What must it do FIRST, and how can AWS help?

choices.text: Move all data to the cheapest storage class, then classify what remains
Encrypt everything with one KMS key, then decide on classification later
Classify and tag data by sensitivity; Macie helps find it
Apply the strictest controls to all data

Q000468.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Classification decides which controls apply. Tags (for example, classification=confidential) let policies and automation act on it, and Macie helps discover sensitive data that isn't labeled yet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One key first: skips the step that tells you which data needs stronger controls.
• Cheapest storage first: cost optimization before knowing sensitivity risks non-compliance.
• Strictest for everything: costly and often impractical; controls should match sensitivity.

Key takeaway: classify first; controls follow the classification.

Q000474.stem: An auditor asks a company for AWS's SOC 2 report and the AWS PCI DSS attestation, and also asks whether the company's own accounts meet PCI controls. Which services answer each request?

choices.text: AWS Config for AWS's reports; Amazon Inspector for the accounts
Artifact for AWS's reports; Security Hub for the accounts
Security Hub for AWS's reports; AWS Artifact for checking the accounts
Trusted Advisor for both requests

Q000474.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports and agreements. Security Hub's PCI DSS standard checks the customer's accounts against controls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped roles: Security Hub checks your environment; Artifact holds AWS's reports.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks, not compliance reports or PCI mapping.
• Config and Inspector: neither provides AWS audit reports; Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: AWS's compliance evidence → Artifact; your compliance posture → Security Hub/Config.

Q000478.stem: Data flows from browsers to an ALB, from the ALB to EC2, and into RDS. Policy requires encryption everywhere. Which set of controls covers both at rest and in transit?

choices.text: A VPN from browsers to the VPC, with no storage encryption needed
HTTPS on the ALB listener only, plus KMS encryption on RDS
KMS encryption on EBS and RDS, since stored data is where breaches occur
TLS on every hop, plus KMS encryption for EBS and RDS

Q000478.explanation:
Why this is correct:
In transit covers every hop: client to ALB, ALB to targets (HTTPS to targets), and app to database (TLS). At rest covers stored data: EBS volumes and RDS storage with KMS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB listener only: the ALB-to-target and app-to-database hops stay unencrypted.
• Storage only: leaves network hops exposed.
• VPN from browsers: impractical for public users and ignores data at rest.

Key takeaway: list each hop and each store; each needs its own encryption.

Q000482.stem: A product catalog in RDS MySQL is read thousands of times per second and changes a few times per hour. Stale data up to 5 minutes is acceptable. Which design cuts read load MOST?

choices.text: CloudFront in front of the RDS endpoint
A larger RDS instance class with more memory
ElastiCache cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL
Global Accelerator in front of the application

Q000482.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cache-aside layer in ElastiCache serves repeated reads from memory, and a TTL bounds staleness to the acceptable 5 minutes, sharply reducing database queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront: caches HTTP responses at edges; it can't sit in front of a database connection.
• Bigger instance: more capacity, but every read still hits the database.
• Global Accelerator: improves network paths, not database load.

Key takeaway: hot, rarely changing reads with tolerable staleness → cache with a TTL.

Q000485.stem: An app on one EC2 instance hits CPU limits. The team resizes it to a larger type, which requires a stop and start. They now want to handle future growth without downtime. What is the recommended next step?

choices.text: Move the instance to a placement group so it can use more CPU
Scale horizontally: an Auto Scaling group across AZs behind a load balancer
Enable detailed monitoring so the instance can grow its vCPU count automatically
Keep scaling vertically, scheduling a larger instance type each month

Q000485.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The resize was vertical scaling, which has a ceiling and needs a restart. Horizontal scaling adds instances with no downtime and removes the single point of failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Monthly vertical resizes: keep the downtime and the ceiling.
• Detailed monitoring: more frequent metrics; it doesn't change capacity.
• Placement groups: affect network placement, not CPU.

Key takeaway: vertical = bigger box with limits and restarts; horizontal = more boxes.

Q000487.stem: A video platform serves the same 2-10 GB files worldwide from S3 in one Region. Latency is high far from the Region, and egress costs are rising. Which service addresses both issues?

choices.text: CloudFront with the S3 bucket as origin
S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
AWS Global Accelerator in front of the bucket
Cross-Region Replication to every Region

Q000487.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to viewers, reducing latency and origin requests. Transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, and CloudFront delivery is typically cheaper than direct S3 egress.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds uploads (and some downloads) via edges but doesn't cache.
• Replication everywhere: multiplies storage cost and still has no caching.
• Global Accelerator: optimizes TCP/UDP paths to endpoints; it isn't a CDN cache.

Key takeaway: repeatable content for global viewers → CloudFront.

Q000488.stem: One domain must route /api/* to a container service, /images/* to a Lambda function, and requests with header X-Version: beta to a canary group. Which load balancer supports all of this natively?

choices.text: Network Load Balancer with separate listeners on different ports
Gateway Load Balancer with target groups per path
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Application Load Balancer with listener rules

Q000488.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB listener rules match on path, host, and HTTP headers, and ALB supports Lambda functions as targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB: Layer 4, so it can't inspect paths or headers.
• GWLB: for inline network appliances, not HTTP routing.
• CLB: legacy, with no content-based routing.

Key takeaway: HTTP content-based routing (path, host, header) → ALB.

Q000489.stem: A company is designing a three-tier web app that must scale each tier independently, keep the database private, and serve static assets globally. Which mapping fits BEST?

choices.text: CloudFront + S3 and an ALB; app ASG; private Aurora
One large EC2 instance running web, app, and database, behind CloudFront
S3 for the web tier, Route 53 for app logic, and DynamoDB exposed publicly
An ALB in private subnets

Q000489.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each tier scales on its own: the edge serves static files, the ALB spreads traffic, Auto Scaling scales the app tier, and a managed database stays in private subnets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One instance: no independent scaling and a single point of failure.
• Route 53 as app logic: DNS isn't compute, and a public database is exposed.
• Inverted placement: public app servers and databases expose them.

Key takeaway: separate tiers so each scales and is secured independently.

Q000492.stem: Hundreds of Linux instances in three AZs must share a POSIX file system for content that is read often but rarely changed, at the lowest cost. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon S3 mounted as a file system on every instance
Amazon EBS Multi-Attach io2 volumes shared by all instances
FSx for Windows File Server with SMB shares
Amazon EFS with lifecycle to Infrequent Access

Q000492.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS is a regional, multi-AZ POSIX file system mountable by many Linux clients. Lifecycle management moves colder files to the lower-cost Infrequent Access class.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS Multi-Attach: limited to a few instances in one AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system.
• S3 as a file system: not POSIX-compliant; mount tools have semantic limitations.
• FSx for Windows: SMB for Windows workloads, not the natural fit for Linux POSIX sharing.

Key takeaway: shared POSIX files across AZs → EFS; cost → lifecycle to IA.

Q000493.stem: A self-managed database on EC2 needs 60,000 IOPS with consistent sub-millisecond latency on one volume and 99.999% durability. Which storage fits BEST?

choices.text: EBS io2 Block Express
EC2 instance store NVMe volumes
EBS gp3 at 60,000 IOPS
Amazon EFS in Max I/O mode

Q000493.explanation:
Why this is correct:
io2 Block Express supports very high IOPS per volume with consistent sub-millisecond latency and 99.999% durability, which suits critical databases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp3: supports up to 16,000 IOPS per volume.
• EFS: a network file system with higher latency, not block storage for a single database.
• Instance store: fast but ephemeral; data is lost if the instance stops or fails.

Key takeaway: highest, most consistent block performance plus durability → io2 Block Express.

Q000494.stem: An ECS workload must always run 4 copies of a task behind an ALB, replace failed tasks, and roll out new versions gradually. Which ECS construct provides this?

choices.text: A task definition with 4 container definitions
An ECS service with desired count 4 and a load balancer
The ECS container agent's restart policy on each instance
A standalone RunTask call scheduled every minute

Q000494.explanation:
Why this is correct:
An ECS service maintains the desired number of running tasks, replaces failed ones, registers them with the load balancer, and manages rolling or blue/green deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scheduled RunTask: launches tasks but doesn't maintain a count or integrate with deployments.
• Four containers in one task definition: that's one task with four containers, not four copies.
• Agent restart policy: restarts containers on one instance, not service-level replacement or deployments.

Key takeaway: long-running, self-healing, load-balanced tasks → ECS service.

Q000497.stem: A company wants a database to survive the loss of a single data center facility with automatic failover, but keep synchronous replication latency low. Across which boundary should it replicate?

choices.text: Across AWS Regions
Across Availability Zones
Across racks in one Availability Zone
Across edge locations

Q000497.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power and networking, connected by low-latency links, which is the right boundary for synchronous high availability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Across Regions: much higher latency; used for DR with async replication.
• Edge locations: don't host databases.
• Racks in one AZ: an AZ-level event takes them all down.

Key takeaway: synchronous HA boundary = Availability Zone.

Q000499.stem: An accessibility feature must read support articles aloud in several languages, with some words pronounced in a custom way, and generate audio files cached for reuse. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabularies
Amazon Comprehend with custom entities
Amazon Polly with custom lexicons
Amazon Translate with custom terminology

Q000499.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Polly converts text to speech in many languages. Lexicons control pronunciation, and synthesized audio can be stored in S3 and reused.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transcribe: speech to text, the opposite direction.
• Translate: text to text between languages; no audio.
• Comprehend: text analytics, no speech output.

Key takeaway: text → speech = Polly; speech → text = Transcribe.

Q000502.stem: An app needs RPO in minutes and RTO under an hour at low cost. The plan: keep a replica database running in a second Region and provision app servers from AMIs only during a disaster. Which DR strategy is this?

choices.text: Multi-site active-active
Warm standby
Pilot light
Backup and restore

Q000502.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pilot light keeps only the core data layer running and replicated; the rest is provisioned quickly during failover. This gives minutes of RPO and a sub-hour RTO at low standing cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully running stack.
• Backup and restore: nothing runs; data is restored from backups, so recovery is slower.
• Active-active: full capacity in both Regions.

Key takeaway: only data running = pilot light; everything running small = warm standby.

Q000506.stem: A payment service calls a partner API that sometimes returns 503. Retries currently happen immediately in a loop, worsening the outage. The team also wants to stop calling after sustained failures. Which combination fits?

choices.text: Fan-out to three copies of the request
Backoff with jitter plus a circuit breaker
Immediate retries with a higher attempt limit
A bulkhead that doubles the thread pool

Q000506.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backoff with jitter spreads retries so a recovering service isn't overwhelmed. A circuit breaker stops calls after repeated failures and probes later, protecting both sides during extended outages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More immediate retries: amplifies load during an outage.
• Fan-out: triples load on the failing dependency.
• Bigger bulkhead: isolates resources but doesn't reduce retry pressure.

Key takeaway: transient → backoff with jitter; sustained → circuit breaker.

Q000507.stem: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance's primary fails. The application uses the RDS endpoint name but caches DNS results for 1 hour. What happens, and what should be fixed?

choices.text: RDS promotes a read replica with a new endpoint that must be configured
The standby serves reads during failover, so no change is needed
RDS fails over and updates the endpoint's DNS; fix the app's DNS caching
The application must restore from a snapshot, since Multi-AZ doesn't fail over automatically

Q000507.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ fails over to the synchronous standby automatically and repoints the same DNS name. Clients that cache DNS longer than the record's short TTL keep connecting to the old IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Read replica promotion: that's a manual pattern with a new endpoint, not Multi-AZ.
• Snapshot restore: Multi-AZ fails over automatically.
• Standby serving reads: a Multi-AZ DB instance standby isn't readable.

Key takeaway: Multi-AZ changes the IP behind the same name, so clients must respect DNS TTL.

Q000509.stem: A team patches servers by SSH, and servers slowly drift apart. They want every change to be versioned, tested, and easy to roll back. Which practice fits BEST?

choices.text: Manual hotfixes recorded in a change log
Immutable infrastructure with pipeline-built AMIs
Snapshots of each server before every SSH change
Rolling in-place updates with a configuration management agent

Q000509.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable infrastructure bakes changes into a new, versioned image (for example, EC2 Image Builder) and replaces instances, so there's no drift, tests run on the exact image, and rollback means redeploying the previous image.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-place updates: still mutate running servers, so drift can creep in.
• Manual hotfixes: the cause of the problem.
• Snapshots: help recovery, but changes are still manual and untested.

Key takeaway: never patch in place; replace with a new, versioned image.

Q000512.stem: A Lambda-based API opens many connections to Aurora. During failover, connections fail and the app returns errors for about 30 seconds. Which change reduces the impact MOST?

choices.text: Add more Aurora Replicas in the same AZ
Increase the Lambda timeout to 60 seconds
Enable Aurora Backtrack on the cluster
Disable Multi-AZ to avoid failovers
RDS Proxy between Lambda and Aurora

Q000512.explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS Proxy pools connections and keeps client connections open while it reconnects to the new writer, cutting perceived failover time and preventing connection storms from Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer Lambda timeout: requests wait longer but still fail on dropped connections.
• Backtrack: rewinds data; it's unrelated to failover.
• Replicas in one AZ: don't help connection handling and reduce AZ resilience.
• Disabling Multi-AZ: removes high availability.

Key takeaway: connection-heavy clients plus failover → RDS Proxy.

Q000513.stem: A product launch in 3 weeks will need 4x the current EC2 vCPUs and Lambda concurrency. Which step prevents launch-day failures from quotas?

choices.text: Launch in a second Region on the day if the first one hits limits
Delete unused IAM roles to free up EC2 quota
Wait for AWS to raise quotas automatically when usage grows
Request Service Quotas increases now, with usage alarms

Q000513.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Quota increases can take time, so request them ahead of known demand. Service Quotas integrates with CloudWatch usage metrics to alarm before limits are hit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic increases: most quotas don't rise on their own.
• Emergency second Region: complex and risky on launch day.
• Deleting IAM roles: unrelated to EC2 or Lambda quotas.

Key takeaway: plan quotas like capacity, before you need them.

Q000514.stem: A team claims S3 Standard's '11 nines' means data is always accessible. An engineer disagrees. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: 11 nines applies only to S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Standard has 99.9% durability and 11 nines availability
11 nines is durability; Standard's availability design is 99.99%
11 nines covers both durability and availability for S3 Standard

Q000514.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Durability is about not losing objects (99.999999999%). Availability is about being able to access them at a given moment, which S3 Standard designs for 99.99%. Data can be safe but briefly unavailable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both at 11 nines: conflates durability and availability.
• Reversed figures: durability is the 11-nines number.
• One Zone-IA: also designed for 11 nines durability but lower availability, and it's in one AZ.

Key takeaway: durability = won't lose it; availability = can reach it now.

Q000519.stem: Monthly reports are read a few times in the first 30 days, then rarely, but must open in milliseconds when requested. Objects average 50 MB. Which storage plan is MOST cost-effective?

choices.text: S3 One Zone-IA from day one for all reports
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days
S3 Standard for the full retention period
Standard for 30 days, then S3 Standard-IA

Q000519.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standard-IA offers millisecond access at lower storage cost with a per-GB retrieval fee, which fits rarely read data that must still open instantly. Large objects avoid the IA minimum-size charge concern, and a 30-day lifecycle matches IA's minimum storage duration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glacier Flexible Retrieval: retrieval takes minutes to hours.
• Standard throughout: pays higher storage cost for rarely read data.
• One Zone-IA from day one: loses AZ resilience, and IA fees apply during the busy first month.

Key takeaway: rare but instant access → Standard-IA (or Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarer access).

Q000524.stem: A database on a 500 GiB gp2 volume needs more space and IOPS without downtime. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Enable Multi-Attach and attach a second volume for extra IOPS
Elastic Volumes to gp3, then extend the file system
Detach the volume, snapshot it, and restore to a larger volume
Use Data Lifecycle Manager to resize the volume on a schedule

Q000524.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Volumes change size, type, and IOPS on attached volumes without detaching them. The OS file system then needs to be extended to use the new space.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snapshot and restore: works but causes downtime.
• Multi-Attach: shares a volume between instances; it doesn't grow capacity.
• DLM: automates snapshots, not resizing.

Key takeaway: change volume size or type online → Elastic Volumes, then grow the file system.

Q000529.stem: A nightly Spark job processes 300 TB in S3 for 3 hours. The team wants the lowest cost and no idle cluster between runs. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Batch with custom Spark installed on each job container
Amazon Redshift, loading the 300 TB each night before querying
A permanently running EMR cluster
Transient EMR (or EMR Serverless) with Spot task nodes

Q000529.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR runs Spark natively. Creating the cluster per run (or using EMR Serverless) avoids idle costs, and Spot task nodes cut compute cost for interruptible capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent cluster: pays for idle time 21 hours a day.
• Redshift loads: a warehouse, not a Spark engine; loading 300 TB nightly is wasteful.
• Batch with custom Spark: rebuilds what EMR provides.

Key takeaway: big-data frameworks → EMR; batch cadence → transient or serverless.

Q000534.stem: A company must migrate a 3 TB Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL. Stored procedures must be converted, and downtime must be under 15 minutes. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Glue to convert the schema and Kinesis to stream the data
Schema Conversion (SCT) plus DMS full load with CDC
Oracle Data Pump export and import during a weekend outage
Restore an Oracle RMAN backup directly into Aurora

Q000534.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A heterogeneous migration needs schema and code conversion (DMS Schema Conversion or SCT) and a data move with ongoing replication (DMS CDC), so cutover takes minutes once replication lag is near zero.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data Pump: produces Oracle-format dumps and requires long downtime.
• Glue and Kinesis: not a migration toolkit for schema and code conversion.
• RMAN into Aurora: Oracle backups can't be restored into PostgreSQL.

Key takeaway: heterogeneous plus low downtime → schema conversion + DMS CDC.

Q000539.stem: A single ALB serves api.example.com and www.example.com. On api, /v2/* must go to a new target group; everything else goes to the old one. Which listener rule configuration fits?

choices.text: Cross-zone load balancing with two target groups
Sticky sessions on the new target group
Two separate ALBs with a Route 53 weighted record
Host and path conditions in ordered rules

Q000539.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB rules can combine host header and path conditions, evaluated in priority order, so api.example.com + /v2/* reaches the new group and other traffic falls through to later rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two ALBs: unnecessary cost, and DNS weighting can't route by path.
• Sticky sessions: bind users to targets; no routing logic.
• Cross-zone: balances across AZs; no content routing.

Key takeaway: host and path conditions with rule priorities.

Q000541.stem: The database in a three-tier VPC must download OS patches from the internet but must never accept inbound internet connections. It must also be reachable only from the app tier. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: Private subnet with a route to the internet gateway for patches
Private subnet with no outbound path and patches copied in manually
Public subnet with an Elastic IP and a security group that blocks all inbound
Private subnet via a NAT gateway, with an SG allowing only the app tier's SG

Q000541.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway provides outbound-only internet access for private subnets, and a security group that references the app tier's group allows only that tier to connect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public subnet with an EIP: directly addressable from the internet; one misconfiguration exposes it.
• IGW route from a private subnet: makes it public.
• No outbound path: blocks the stated patching requirement.

Key takeaway: outbound only → NAT; inbound only from one tier → SG referencing that tier's SG.

Q000544.stem: A multiplayer game uses UDP and a custom TCP protocol, needs to see client source IPs, and must support millions of connections with static IPs per AZ. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Classic Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer

Q000544.explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB handles TCP and UDP at Layer 4 with very high throughput, preserves client source IPs, and supports a static IP or Elastic IP per AZ.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB: HTTP/HTTPS only.
• GWLB: for inserting network appliances, not client traffic distribution.
• CLB: legacy, with no UDP support.

Key takeaway: non-HTTP, source IP preservation, static IPs → NLB.

Q000548.stem: 200 TB on an on-premises NFS server must be copied to S3 over a 10 Gbps link, followed by nightly incremental syncs with integrity checks, preserving metadata. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Direct Connect alone, mounting S3 as NFS
S3 Transfer Acceleration with aws s3 sync
AWS Snowball Edge devices every night
AWS DataSync with an on-premises agent

Q000548.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataSync transfers from NFS or SMB to S3 efficiently, verifies integrity, handles incremental runs on a schedule, and preserves metadata. At 10 Gbps, 200 TB is feasible online in a few days.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snowball nightly: physical devices suit one-time bulk moves, not daily increments.
• Transfer Acceleration with sync: no built-in scheduling or integrity reporting, and acceleration targets long-distance paths.
• Direct Connect alone: a network link, not a transfer tool, and S3 isn't an NFS server.

Key takeaway: online, repeatable, verified file transfer → DataSync.

Q000549.stem: Analysts need ad hoc SQL over 50 TB of Parquet in S3, with no servers to manage, and shared interactive dashboards with row-level security by region. Which combination fits BEST?

choices.text: A permanently running EMR cluster with Hive and Grafana
Glue crawlers alone for both querying and dashboards
Load all data into RDS for PostgreSQL and use SNS for dashboards
Athena for SQL, QuickSight with row-level security

Q000549.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena queries S3 data serverlessly with pay-per-scan pricing, which is ideal for Parquet. QuickSight builds shared dashboards and supports row-level security.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EMR and Grafana: servers to run and no native row-level security for business users.
• RDS and SNS: loading 50 TB into RDS is impractical, and SNS isn't a dashboard tool.
• Glue crawlers: build the catalog but don't run queries or dashboards.

Key takeaway: serverless SQL on S3 → Athena; BI dashboards → QuickSight.

Q000550.stem: Five teams need access to shared S3 data lake tables: some columns (for example, salary) must be hidden from most teams, and some rows filtered by country. Permissions must be managed centrally. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: IAM policies listing allowed column names
AWS Lake Formation with column and row filters
Separate S3 bucket policies per team and prefix
Amazon Macie with sensitive data findings

Q000550.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation grants table-, column-, and row-level permissions (data filters) centrally, enforced for integrated engines such as Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policies: object-level only; can't filter columns or rows.
• IAM policies: can't restrict columns in query results.
• Macie: finds sensitive data; doesn't control access.

Key takeaway: fine-grained data lake access → Lake Formation.

Q000555.stem: A public research dataset in S3 is downloaded heavily by outside institutions with AWS accounts. The owner wants downloaders to pay for request and transfer costs, and wants to block anonymous access. Which setting fits?

choices.text: Enable Cross-Region Replication to the users' Regions
Serve the data through CloudFront with signed URLs
Enable Requester Pays
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration

Q000555.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With Requester Pays, the requester pays for requests and data transfer. Requests must be authenticated, so anonymous downloads aren't allowed, which matches the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds transfers and adds cost to the owner.
• Replication: adds storage cost for the owner.
• CloudFront signed URLs: control access, but the owner still pays delivery costs.

Key takeaway: shift download costs to requesters → Requester Pays.

Q000557.stem: A team wants an email when forecast monthly spend will exceed $10,000, and also wants a Slack alert when actual spend passes 80% of that budget. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Cost and Usage Report delivered to S3
AWS Budgets forecast and actual alerts
AWS Cost Explorer saved reports
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks

Q000557.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Budgets supports thresholds on forecast and actual spend and notifies through email or SNS, which can feed Slack via AWS Chatbot.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer: analysis, not proactive alerts.
• CUR: detailed billing data files; no alerting.
• Trusted Advisor: optimization tips; no budget alerts.

Key takeaway: thresholds and alerts on spend → Budgets.

Q000559.stem: A database needs a steady 6,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s on a 400 GiB volume at the lowest cost. Which EBS configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: gp2 at 2 TiB to earn the IOPS from size
st1 throughput-optimized HDD
io2 with 6,000 provisioned IOPS
gp3 with provisioned IOPS and throughput

Q000559.explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of size at a lower price than io2, and 6,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s are within its limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp2 at 2 TiB: pays for unneeded capacity to get IOPS.
• io2: meets it but costs more; its extra durability and latency consistency aren't required here.
• st1: HDD for sequential throughput with low IOPS.

Key takeaway: moderate provisioned performance → gp3.

Q000562.stem: A bucket holds 800 million objects averaging 2 MB with unknown, shifting access patterns. Some become hot again after months. The team wants automatic savings with no retrieval fees for the automatic tiers. Which class fits?

choices.text: S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 One Zone-IA

Q000562.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers based on usage and moves them back when accessed, with no retrieval fees for its automatic tiers. A small monitoring fee per object applies, which is acceptable at 2 MB average size.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard-IA: retrieval fees add up when objects become hot again.
• Glacier Flexible Retrieval: slow retrieval.
• One Zone-IA: less resilient, and it has retrieval fees.

Key takeaway: unknown or changing access → Intelligent-Tiering.

Q000563.stem: A video transcoding queue can pause and resume jobs from checkpoints, with no deadline tighter than 24 hours. Which EC2 purchasing strategy minimizes cost while limiting interruptions?

choices.text: Standard Reserved Instances for peak capacity
On-Demand Instances of one instance type
Diversified Spot, price-capacity-optimized
Dedicated Hosts purchased for three years

Q000563.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot provides the largest discount for interruptible work, and diversifying instance types and AZs with price-capacity-optimized allocation draws from deep pools to reduce interruptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand: pays full price for flexible work.
• Dedicated Hosts: expensive and meant for licensing or compliance needs.
• Reserved for peak: commits to capacity idle most of the time.

Key takeaway: interruptible and flexible → diversified Spot.

Q000566.stem: A company runs 25 HTTP microservices. It wants one entry point with path routing, TLS termination with ACM, and authentication against an OIDC provider at the load balancer, at low cost. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: One ALB with path rules and OIDC auth
A Network Load Balancer per microservice
A Classic Load Balancer per microservice
A Gateway Load Balancer with 25 target groups

Q000566.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single ALB can hold many listener rules for path routing, terminate TLS with ACM, and authenticate users through OIDC or Cognito, so one load balancer covers all services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB per service: 25 load balancers, and no path routing or OIDC.
• CLB: legacy, with no path routing or OIDC.
• GWLB: for network appliances, not HTTP routing.

Key takeaway: many HTTP services behind one entry point → one ALB with rules.

Q000575.stem: A regulated app must keep 10 years of transactions queryable on demand, but rows older than 2 years are rarely read. The RDS database is growing expensively. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Delete rows older than 2 years
Increase the RDS storage size for all 10 years
Archive old rows to S3 and query with Athena
Move the database to a larger instance class

Q000575.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exporting old data to S3 in a columnar format keeps it cheap and durable while still queryable on demand with Athena, and the primary database shrinks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger storage: keeps paying database prices for cold data.
• Deleting: violates the 10-year retention requirement.
• Bigger instance: adds compute cost without addressing storage.

Key takeaway: hot data in the database, cold data in S3 with query-in-place.

Q000578.stem: A new RDS database needs 8,000 IOPS steadily and can tolerate occasional latency variation. Cost matters. Which storage option fits BEST?

choices.text: io1 storage, since production databases require Provisioned IOPS
io2 Block Express for the lowest possible latency
Magnetic storage, since it's the cheapest option
gp3 storage with 8,000 provisioned IOPS

Q000578.explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 lets you provision IOPS separately from size at lower cost. io1 and io2 are for workloads that need very high IOPS or the most consistent latency, which isn't required here.

Why the other options are wrong:
• io1: pricier and not required for production by any rule.
• Magnetic: legacy, with low performance.
• io2 Block Express: exceeds the need at higher cost.

Key takeaway: pick the cheapest storage that meets the performance requirement.

Q000580.stem: A non-production VPC has NAT gateways in three AZs, and costs are high. Some downtime of outbound access during an AZ failure is acceptable, and cross-AZ data charges should stay low. Which change fits BEST?

choices.text: Add a second NAT gateway in each AZ for redundancy
One NAT gateway plus S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints
Replace the NAT gateways with an egress-only internet gateway
Route the private subnets directly to the internet gateway

Q000580.explanation:
Why this is correct:
One NAT gateway cuts the hourly cost by two thirds, accepting reduced resilience in non-production. Gateway endpoints remove S3 and DynamoDB traffic from the NAT path, reducing processing and cross-AZ charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More NAT gateways: increases cost.
• Direct IGW routes: makes subnets public.
• Egress-only gateway: IPv6 only.

Key takeaway: match redundancy to environment criticality, and remove traffic from NAT where endpoints exist.

Q000582.stem: A company wants example.com (the zone apex) to point to an ALB and cdn.example.com to CloudFront, without paying for those DNS queries. Which record types fit?

choices.text: CNAME records for both names
TXT records containing the target DNS names
Alias A (and AAAA) records for both names
A CNAME for cdn and an A record with the ALB's IP for the apex

Q000582.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alias records work at the zone apex, track the target's changing IPs, and queries to alias records pointing at AWS resources are free.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNAMEs: not allowed at the zone apex, and CNAME queries are billed.
• Hardcoded ALB IP: ALB IPs change.
• TXT records: don't route traffic.

Key takeaway: AWS targets and zone apex → alias records.

Q000585.stem: FinOps must build a custom allocation model using per-resource, hourly line items for data transfer and NAT charges over the last 3 months, queried with SQL. Which source fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Budgets reports emailed weekly
CUR in S3, queried with Athena
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
Cost Explorer grouped by service

Q000585.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CUR (or Data Exports) delivers the most detailed billing data, including resource IDs and hourly granularity, to S3, where Athena can query it with SQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets reports: summaries against thresholds.
• Cost Explorer: aggregated views without full line-item detail for custom models.
• Trusted Advisor: recommendations, not billing data.

Key takeaway: line-item billing analytics → CUR + Athena.
